1.content:
Conclusion: VM Performance is low because the VM is waiting on memory-tiering NVMe fetches; the added metrics do not change that.

Mechanism and reason
* VM Performance % is a contention KPI. Its memory-wait component is Peak memory wait = VM Memory Contention + NVMe wait on tiered hosts. `vsphere/object-types/vm/vm-performance`
* VM Memory Contention maps to VM Memory Latency, which is unaware of memory tiering and does not count NVMe fetches. `vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/virtual-motherboard/latency`
* NVMe wait is added by Little’s law: VM NVMe read bandwidth ×256 × host NVMe read latency / vCPUs ×100. With 6 MBps, 290 µs, 8 vCPUs the estimate is ≈5.6% of vCPU time. That wait is part of the VM Performance memory-wait sub-metric and is absent from Memory Contention and from CPU Ready, which are near zero.
* VM CPU Net Run = Run – Overlap is a sizing/capacity input, not a contention wait. It does not create a wait and is unrelated to the memory-wait component that is pulling the KPI down. `vsphere/technology/cpu/metrics/virtual-motherboard/net-run`
* ESXi Memory Consumed is host memory use including cache and kernel; near 100% is normal in an overcommitted host and it is a capacity metric, not a VM-wait metric. It does not explain VM Performance and is not used in the VM Performance formula. `vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/host/consumed`

What to check next
* Host esxi-pay-05 tier metrics: Tier memory consumed, Tier in rate, Active memory % of DRAM, and NVMe read latency trend; confirm sustained NVMe reads and whether the working set no longer fits DRAM. `vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/memory-tiering`
* Per-VM NVMe read bandwidth for pay-api-07 over the 20-second peak window that matches the 17% score, and whether the VM should be excluded from tiering with a full reservation. `vsphere/technology/memory/decision-tree/is-memory-tiering-slowing-host`
* Other VM Performance sub-metrics: Peak CPU Co-stop, Peak CPU Overlap, Disk Latency, Network Dropped Tx, and CPU Net Run as context for utilization, not as a cause. `vsphere/object-types/vm/vm-performance`

Assumption: the 290 µs NVMe read latency is the relevant host value for the period of the 17% score; interval/baseline is not given.
computed: - NVMe wait of VM = 6 MBps x 256 pages per MB x 290 µs / 8 vCPUs = 5.6% of its vCPU time. [arithmetic_calculator.py: NVMe wait (%) = VM NVMe read bandwidth (MB/s) x 256 pages per MB x host NVMe read latency (s) / VM vCPUs x 100 (Little's law). It assumes one 4 KB page per fetch and that the fetch stalls the vCPU; if either fails, it overstates the wait. Memory Contention does not count this wait. See vsphere/object-types/cluster/cluster-performance, section Sub-metric formulas.]

2.content:
Conclusion: The NVMe read is sustained, not a warm-up. The working set no longer fits the DRAM left to the tiered VMs, and memory tiering is slowing the host.

Mechanism and reason
* NVMe is active: consumed grew 0 → 50 GB Fri 18:00 → 280 GB Tue 08:00. Tiering started, pages were demoted over the weekend with write bandwidth up and read bandwidth ~0 Fri 18:00–Tue 08:30.
* Active memory against DRAM is the leading capacity signal on a tiered host. Host esxi-pay-05 has 1,024 GB DRAM. Active memory 790 GB at 09:10 and 785 GB at 10:15 ≈ 77% of DRAM. The decision tree sets >75% as significant loss expected, and 50-75% as at risk; Active is above 75% here. `vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/virtual-motherboard/active`
* Warm-up vs sustained is decided by NVMe read bandwidth persistence after the first busy hour. The flow says: after an idle period reads fetch cold pages back; read the bandwidth again at least an hour later. At or below 200 MB/s = warm-up; still >200 MB/s = sustained: working set no longer fits DRAM left. `vsphere/technology/memory/decision-tree/is-memory-tiering-slowing-host`
  09:10 = 380 MBps, 10:15 = 360 MBps, 65 min apart, both >200 MBps. The computed flow row confirms sustained: working set no longer fits the DRAM left.
* NVMe read latency 290 µs / 280 µs is in the 200-400 µs “potential issues” band. With sustained reads the VMs incur NVMe wait ≈ reads × latency.

What to check next
* Per-VM NVMe read bandwidth to identify the VMs paying the wait.
* Trend of NVMe read bandwidth beyond 10:15 to confirm it does not fall below 200 MB/s.
* NVMe read IOPS / hit rate and workload identity / memory access pattern.
* VCF 9.1.1 tiering policy and warm-up settings, and baseline NVMe read bandwidth for normal business hours.

Knowledge base: `vsphere/technology/memory/decision-tree/is-memory-tiering-slowing-host`, `vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/virtual-motherboard/active`.

3.content:
Conclusion: sql-pay-03 with tiering disabled and a full 256 GB reservation pins 256 GB of DRAM and removes that DRAM from the pool available to tiered VMs on esxi-pay-05, which drives the host active % up and forces tiered VMs to fetch from NVMe.

Mechanism and reason
Memory tiering capacity is decided by Active memory against DRAM, not by ESXi Memory Usage. ESXi Memory Usage maps to ESXi Memory Consumed = Consumed/Total Capacity and is a capacity reporting metric; pressure shows in ballooning, compression, swapping and VM Memory Contention, not in Usage %. vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/host/usage
Tiering starts ~80 % DRAM consumption; hot pages stay in DRAM, cold pages go to NVMe. A VM with sched.mem.enableTiering=FALSE is excluded from tiering. With a full reservation its memory stays in DRAM and the reservation is a floor against reclamation. Each DRAM-only reservation shrinks the DRAM left for tiered VMs, lowering the effective DRAM:NVMe ratio. vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/memory-tiering
esxi-pay-05: 1 024 GB DRAM + 1 024 GB NVMe, Active 785 GB = 77 % of DRAM. Guidance is ≤50 % green, 50-75 % at risk, >75 % significant loss expected. NVMe read bandwidth 360 MBps >200 MBps watch level, NVMe read latency 280 µs = 200-400 µs potential issues. vsphere/technology/memory/decision-tree/is-memory-tiering-slowing-host
sql-pay-03 is 256 GB reserved, tiering off, active 110 GB. The 256 GB is pinned in DRAM, so tiered VMs effectively have ~768 GB DRAM vs 1 024 GB NVMe ≈0.75:1. The high active % and NVMe reads/latency are the symptom of the working set no longer fitting the DRAM left to tiered VMs. Hosts esxi-pay-07/08 without the SQL VM show 44 %/41 % active and ~30 MBps NVMe reads.

What to check next
Per-VM NVMe read bandwidth to find which tiered VMs, especially the 5 payments VMs, are waiting on NVMe; host tier consumed mem.tier.consumed and per-VM tier1Consumed; confirm the reservation is hard/full and whether sql-pay-03 can be moved off the tiered host or have tiering re-enabled with a reduced reservation to restore DRAM for the tiered pool.

4.content:
Cluster memory headroom is not given by VCF Operations Memory Capacity Remaining on a tiered cluster. The premise that the two metrics should agree is wrong.

Mechanism and reason
* Memory Capacity Remaining % is VCF Operations 3-Day Forecast Capacity Remaining: usable capacity minus the highest projected utilization in the next 3 days, the tightest point of the projection. `vcf-operations/features/capacity-forecast`
* On a memory-tiered host VCF Operations counts the NVMe tier in Total Memory Capacity. Capacity Remaining and Time Remaining therefore treat NVMe as if it were DRAM and overstate supply. The guidance is to read active memory against DRAM and tier consumption instead. `vcf-operations/features/capacity-forecast`
* Highest ESXi DRAM Memory Consumed is the Cluster Risk sub-metric: memory consumed in DRAM and NVMe as % of host DRAM. It passes 100 % by design on tiered hosts. 108 % means the host carries 1.08× its DRAM, the excess in NVMe. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk`
* The capacity constraint with tiering moves from Consumed to Active memory. Consumed may exceed DRAM; Active must stay within DRAM, ideally <50 %. `vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/memory-tiering`
  Today Worst ESXi Active Memory, tiered hosts = 77 % of DRAM. That is >75 % where significant performance loss is expected, and >50 % where it is at risk. NVMe read latency is 290 µs today, above the <200 µs good threshold and in the 200-400 µs potential-issues band. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk`; `vsphere/technology/memory/concepts/memory-tiering`

What to check next
* Active memory per host vs DRAM, NVMe read bandwidth and per-VM NVMe read bandwidth, and whether hosts are warming up after idle periods. 
* Ballooned/compressed/swapped memory and per-VM memory contention; on a tiered host contention does not count NVMe waits. 
* Monster VMs and reservations that reduce DRAM left for tiered VMs.

The 108 % is the tiering effect, not a DRAM overcommit in the planning sense; the cluster is already memory-pressured on the DRAM tier.

5.content:
Cluster Risk is the risk model, not a KPI, higher is worse. It warns of potential contention before VMs feel it; 66% is orange. Every sub-metric takes the worst ESXi host, one full host hurts while cluster average looks fine. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk`

* Cluster Risk % 66.0
Tells potential contention risk now. It is 100 − weighted average of the 12 sub-metrics, worst host. Orange = 50-75. It is a leading indicator; Cluster Performance shows actual contention now. Risk can rise days before performance drops. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk`

* Highest ESXi Memory Reservation % 26
Per host reserved memory / host DRAM. Reservation is a guarantee and cannot be overcommitted; admission control checks reservations, never usage. 26% yellow from 23:25 last Tuesday means more reserved capacity is locked, reducing usable capacity and raising risk. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk` `vsphere/architecture/resource-controls`

* Highest ESXi DRAM Memory Consumed % 108
Memory consumed in DRAM and NVMe as % of host DRAM. On a tiered host it passes 100% by design. Measured against DRAM only, NVMe never added to the base. 108% red today, yellow from Friday 08:40, is a leading risk signal, not contention. Near 100% is normal; pressure shows in ballooning/compression/swapping and VM Memory Contention. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk` `vsphere/technology/memory/metrics/host/usage`

* Highest ESXi Memory Overcommit Ratio 1.23
Allocation / supply: memory of powered-on VMs / host DRAM. Only allocation can be overcommitted. Ratio says nothing about performance by itself; contention does. Stepped up Thursday 23:35. `sp5-framework/capacity/overcommit` `vsphere/object-types/cluster/models/cluster-risk`

* Highest ESXi CPU Overcommit Ratio 1.41
vCPUs of powered-on VMs per physical thread. CPU executes per thread, so with Hyper-Threading 3:1 per thread = 6:1 per core. Stepped up Thursday 23:35. `sp5-framework/capacity/overcommit`

* Cluster Performance % 48
Cluster KPI, higher is better. Depth from worst VM, breadth from 90th percentile, aggregated from VMs at 20-second peaks. 48% orange means actual contention is happening now. It is the only cluster KPI; Cluster Risk is a risk model. `vsphere/object-types/cluster/cluster-performance`

Next: read the Cluster Risk sub-metrics for the worst host, identify which host changed Thursday 23:35 and Tuesday 23:25, check reservations, monster VMs and VM Memory Contention; do not act on the falling/rising score alone.
